doc.title: Johnny Varro interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001

chapter: Condon's circle and New York scene
title: Drinking among jazz musicians
summary: Why jazz and drinking go together, and his own insecurity and drinking while playing.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: Well I hear, I mean I’ve read of course that he was a major league drinker.
Yeah, a lot of them. A lot of the guys. Most of the guys were.
Is there a reason that jazz is associated with that? I mean is it as simple as the fact that it’s played in bars?

Yeah I guess that is the main reason. I don’t know, it kind of relaxed you I guess, if you have a couple of snorts you are able to go out and throw caution to the wind and say oh I’m going to hit that high C or I’m going to do that run a little faster or something to that effect. Strangely enough, a lot of musicians are insecure to begin with. I shouldn’t say a lot because — speaking for myself I felt insecure at the time. I wasn’t sure that I qualified to be playing with all these guys. So maybe a couple of drinks would loosen me up and I’d feel better about it myself you know. Sometimes it would hurt you too. If I did a recording when I was having too much to drink it wouldn’t turn out as good as I thought it was at the time. So you had to be careful about that. Trial and error.
